Mesillat Yesharim 16:16: And indeed, this is truly the test by which the servants of the Lord themselves are tested and distinguished according to their level, for whoever knows how to purify his heart more, he is the one who draws nearer and is more beloved by Him, blessed be He. These are the first ones who were in the land, who prevailed and were victorious in this matter — the Patriarchs and the other shepherds who purified their hearts before Him. This is what David warns his son Solomon (I Chronicles 28:9): "for the Lord searches all hearts, and understands every inclination of the thoughts."
Mesillat Yesharim 16:17: And so they said, of blessed memory (Sanhedrin 106b): the Merciful One desires the heart.
Mesillat Yesharim 16:18: For the deeds alone are not enough for the Master, blessed be He, that they merely be deeds of a commandment; rather, the essential thing before Him is that the heart be pure, directing its intention toward true service.
Mesillat Yesharim 16:19: And behold, the heart is the king over all the parts of the body, and directs them; and if it does not bring itself to His service, blessed be He, the service of the other limbs is worthless, for they will go wherever the spirit of the heart leads them. And Scripture says explicitly (Proverbs 23:26): "Give Me, my son, your heart."
Mesillat Yesharim 17:1:
The Ways of Acquiring Purity
Now, the way to attain this trait is easy for one who has already striven for and attained the traits discussed up to now. For when he thinks and reflects on the lowliness of the world's pleasures and its goods, as I have written above, he will despise them and consider them nothing but evils and deficiencies of dark and coarse material nature. And once it becomes clear to him that they are truly deficiencies and evils, it will certainly become easier for him to separate himself from them and to remove them from his heart.
Mesillat Yesharim 17:2: Therefore, the more deeply and persistently he recognizes the lowliness of materiality and its pleasures, the easier it will be for him to purify his thoughts and his heart, so as not to turn to the inclination at all in any of his actions, but rather to be, in material actions, like one under compulsion, and nothing more.
Mesillat Yesharim 17:3: And indeed, just as we divided purity of thought into two parts — one in bodily actions, and one in acts of service — so the reflection needed to acquire it likewise divides into two:
Mesillat Yesharim 17:4: For to purify his thought in his bodily actions, the way is to persist in contemplating the lowliness of the world and its pleasures, as I have written. And to purify his thought in his acts of service, he should increase his reflection on the deceptiveness of honor and its falseness, and accustom himself to flee from it.
Mesillat Yesharim 17:5: Then, at the time of his service, he will become cleansed of turning toward the praise and glory with which people would praise him, and his thought will be directed solely toward our Master, who is our praise, and who is all our good and our perfection, with nothing besides Him. And so it says (Deuteronomy 10:21): "He is your praise, and He is your God."
Mesillat Yesharim 17:6: And among the practices that guide a person to attain this trait is preparation for matters of service and the commandments — that is, that he should not enter into the performance of a commandment suddenly, all at once, while his mind is not yet settled and able to reflect on what he is doing, but rather he should prepare himself for the matter and ready his heart calmly, until he enters into it with proper reflection.
Mesillat Yesharim 17:7: And then he should reflect on what he is about to do, and before whom he is about to do it; for once he enters into this reflection, it will be easy for him to cast off external considerations and to fix in his heart the true, desired intention.
Mesillat Yesharim 17:8: And you will see that the early pious ones would tarry one hour before their prayer and then pray, in order to direct their hearts to the Omnipresent. And certainly they did not spend that hour idly, but rather they were intending and preparing their hearts for the prayer they were about to pray, driving away foreign thoughts and filling themselves with the necessary fear and love. And it is said (Job 11:13): "If you set your heart aright, and spread out your hands toward Him..."
Mesillat Yesharim 17:9: Now, the things that undermine this trait are a lack of reflection on the matters we have mentioned — namely: foolishness regarding the lowliness of pleasures, the pursuit of honor, and insufficient preparation for service.
Mesillat Yesharim 17:10: For the first two entice the mind and draw it toward outside considerations, like an adulterous woman who, in place of her husband, takes strangers. And outside thoughts have already been called "the harlotry of the heart," as it is written (Numbers 15:39): "and you shall not go about after your own heart and after your own eyes, after which you go astray." For the heart is found turning away from the complete gaze to which it should be bound, toward vanities and false imaginings.
Mesillat Yesharim 17:11: And insufficient preparation causes the natural foolishness that comes from materiality not to be driven out from within, so that it makes the service foul with its stench.
Mesillat Yesharim 17:12: Let us now explain the trait of piety.
Mesillat Yesharim 18:1:
An Explanation of the Trait of Piety (Chasidut)
The trait of piety truly requires great explanation, for many customs and many ways pass among many people under the name of piety, while they are nothing but shapeless lumps of piety, without form, without shape, and without refinement,
Mesillat Yesharim 18:2: and this results from the lack of true reflection and understanding among those who hold these traits, for they did not trouble themselves and did not labor to know the way of the Lord with clear and straight knowledge, but rather practiced piety and went about according to whatever occurred to them by their first impression, without probing deeply into matters or weighing them in the scales of wisdom.
Mesillat Yesharim 18:3: And behold, these have given piety a bad name in the eyes of the masses, and even among the intelligent among them, since they now think that piety depends on vain matters, or things contrary to reason and correct understanding, and they believe that all piety depends merely on saying many supplications, great confessions, weeping and prostrations, and on strange self-mortifications by which a person nearly kills himself — such as immersions in ice and snow and similar things.
Mesillat Yesharim 18:4: And behold, they did not know that although some of these things are needed by penitents, and some are fitting for the abstinent, piety itself was not founded on these at all — rather, the good part of these practices is fitting to accompany piety.
Mesillat Yesharim 18:5: But the essence of piety itself is a matter very deep to understand correctly, and it is founded upon the foundations of great wisdom and the perfecting of deeds to the utmost degree, which every person wise of heart should pursue, for only the wise can truly attain it. And so they said, of blessed memory (Avot 2:5): "nor is an ignorant person pious."
Mesillat Yesharim 18:6: Let us now explain this matter in order.
Mesillat Yesharim 18:7: Behold, the root of piety is what they said, of blessed memory (Berachot 17a): "Happy is the man whose labor is in Torah, and who gives satisfaction to his Maker."
Mesillat Yesharim 18:8: And the matter is that the commandments incumbent upon all of Israel are already known, and their obligation is known as to how far it extends.
Mesillat Yesharim 18:9: However, whoever loves the Creator, blessed be His Name, with a true love, will not strive and intend merely to discharge himself with what is already publicly known as the obligation upon all of Israel in general; rather, what happens to him will be like what happens to a son who loves his father: if his father were to reveal his mind even slightly, that he desires some matter, the son will do much more in that matter and in that deed than he could. And even though his father said it only once and in half a sentence, this is enough for that son to understand where his father's mind leans, to do for him even what he did not explicitly say — since he can judge for himself that this thing will give satisfaction before him, and he does not wait for his father to command him further explicitly or to say it to him again.
Mesillat Yesharim 18:10: And behold, we see this with our own eyes, that this is born at every time and every hour between every loving friend, between a man and his wife, between a father and his son,
Mesillat Yesharim 18:11: in sum, between anyone whose love for one another is truly intense — that he will not say, "I was not commanded more; it is enough for me what I was explicitly commanded," but rather, from what he was commanded, he will judge the mind of the one who commanded him, and strive to do for him what he can judge would give him satisfaction.
Mesillat Yesharim 18:12: And behold, this same thing happens to one who loves his Creator with a faithful love as well, for he too is of the category of lovers, and the commandments whose command is revealed and publicly known will serve him only as a disclosure of intent, to know that His will and desire, blessed be His Name, incline toward that matter; and then he will not say, "It is enough for me what is explicitly stated," or "I will discharge myself with what is incumbent upon me in any case," but rather, on the contrary, he will say: since I have already found and seen that His will, blessed be His Name, inclines toward this, it shall be as guiding lights before my eyes to increase in this matter and to extend it in every direction that I can judge that His will, blessed be He, desires it. And this is what is called "giving satisfaction to his Maker."
Mesillat Yesharim 18:13: It follows that the general principle of piety is the extension of the fulfillment of all the commandments in every direction and condition that is fitting and possible.
Mesillat Yesharim 18:14: And you can see that piety is of the same kind as abstinence, except that abstinence concerns the negative commandments and piety concerns the positive commandments, and both are one and the same matter — namely, to add to what is explicitly stated whatever we can judge, according to the explicit commandment, would give satisfaction before Him, blessed be He. This is the definition of true piety.
Mesillat Yesharim 18:15: And now let us explain its principal components.
Mesillat Yesharim 19:1:
An Explanation of the Components of Piety
The primary components of piety are three: the first is in the deed itself, the second in the manner of performing it, the third in the intention.
Mesillat Yesharim 19:2: The first component, in the deed itself, likewise divides into two parts: one concerning what is between man and the Omnipresent, and the other concerning what is between man and his fellow.
Mesillat Yesharim 19:3: The first part of the first component is in the deed that is between man and the Omnipresent, and its matter is the fulfillment of all the commandments in all their fine details, to the extent that is within a person's reach; and these are what our Sages, of blessed memory, called the "remnants of a commandment," and they said (Sukkah 38a): the remnants of a commandment hold back calamity — for even though the essential body of the commandment is complete without them, and one has already discharged his obligation through it, this applies to the masses of Israel in general; but the pious have only to increase in their completion, and not to diminish them at all.
Mesillat Yesharim 19:4: The second part of the first component is in what is between man and his fellow, and its matter is that a person should always be doing good to his fellow creatures and never doing them harm — this applying to body, to money, and to soul.
Mesillat Yesharim 19:5: To the body — that he should strive to help every person as much as he can, and lighten their burdens; this is what we learned (Avot 6:6): "and bears the yoke with his fellow." And if some harm is about to come to his fellow's body, and he is able to prevent it or remove it, he should trouble himself to do so.
Mesillat Yesharim 19:6: To money — to assist him with whatever is within his means, and to prevent damages from him in every way he can, all the more so that he should himself keep far from causing any kind of damage that could come through him, whether to an individual or to the public,
Mesillat Yesharim 19:7: and even if the damage is not immediately present now, since it can come to that eventually, he should remove and eliminate it. And they said, of blessed memory (Avot 2:12): let your fellow's money be as precious to you as your own.
Mesillat Yesharim 19:8: To the soul — that he should strive to give his fellow every satisfaction within his power, whether regarding matters of honor or any other matters; whatever he knows that, if he does it for his fellow, his fellow will receive satisfaction from it, it is a mitzvah of piety to do it; all the more so that he should not cause him any kind of pain at all, in whatever manner it may be.
Mesillat Yesharim 19:9: And the general principle of all this is acts of loving-kindness, whose praise our Sages, of blessed memory, extolled greatly, and our obligation in it; and included in this is the pursuit of peace, which is the general good that applies between every person and his fellow.
